w: Every gum-disease diagnosis starts with three measurements. Probing depth (PD) is how far the probe sinks: from the edge of the gum (the gingival margin) down to the bottom of the pocket. Recession (GR) is how far the gum has pulled back: from the CEJ (the line where enamel meets root) to the gum edge. Clinical attachment level (CAL) is the one that counts for staging. It is the two added together, which works out to the distance from the CEJ down to the bottom of the pocket. It tells you how much of the tooth's real attachment has been lost. The sign matters. If the gum edge sits above the CEJ (so you can't see any root), recession is written as a negative number and CAL comes out smaller than the probing depth. If root is showing, recession is positive and CAL comes out bigger than the probing depth. Example: a 7 mm pocket with the CEJ hiding 4 mm under the gum is only 3 mm of attachment loss. A shallow 2 mm pocket with 4 mm of root showing is 6 mm of attachment loss. The second tooth looks worse on paper, but it is easier to keep, because the patient can actually reach a 2 mm pocket with a brush. X-rays show what a probe can't reach. Use periapicals plus vertical bitewings, not horizontal ones. A horizontal bitewing can miss the bone loss in one of the two jaws completely. A panoramic is a good overview, but it isn't detailed enough to diagnose gum disease by itself. Health, gingivitis, or periodontitis Health: no pocket deeper than 3 mm, no bleeding, no lost attachment, no lost bone. Gingivitis (inflamed gums from plaque) can have 4-5 mm pockets that bleed, but there is no attachment loss and no bone loss. The problem is only in the gums, and it goes away completely once the plaque is controlled. Before calling a mouth "gingivitis," at least 10% of sites should bleed. Probing pressure varies between people, so two or three bleeding spots on their own shouldn't decide it. Periodontitis is different: attachment loss and bone loss are both there, pockets often reach 6 mm or more, and it does not fully reverse. Treatment can stop it, but the best result is healthy gums on a reduced periodontium (less support than the patient started with), not a return to the original attachment. "Intact" or "reduced" describes how much support is left, separately from whether there is disease right now. An intact periodontium can be healthy or have gingivitis. A reduced one (after old periodontitis, crown lengthening, or plain recession) can also be healthy or inflamed. A treated periodontitis patient who stays stable on maintenance is called healthy on a reduced periodontium. You don't re-stage them unless the disease comes back. If pockets deepen and bleeding returns at a later visit, the diagnosis moves back toward periodontitis, depending on how widespread it is. Recession is a sign, not a diagnosis Gums can recede in people who have never had periodontitis, so recession gets its own grading, based on how much attachment is also lost between the teeth. RT1: no loss between the teeth, so the root can be fully covered with surgery. RT2: some loss between the teeth, but less than on the cheek side, so only partial coverage is expected. RT3: more loss between the teeth than on the cheek side, so root coverage isn't tried, because it won't work. Staging and grading Staging answers "how bad is it, and how hard will it be to treat?" The best measure is CAL between the teeth; bone loss on the X-ray is the backup. Stages 1 and 2 are early: more attachment loss, but bone loss still in the top third of the root. Stages 3 and 4 both have CAL of 5 mm or more and bone loss into the middle third or deeper. What separates 3 from 4 is not more attachment loss. It is how many teeth were lost to gum disease (4 or fewer is Stage 3, 5 or more is Stage 4) and whether the case needs complex, multi-specialty rebuilding. Three findings jump a case straight to Stage 3 or 4 no matter what the CAL says: vertical (angular) bone loss of 3 mm or more, a Class II or III furcation (bone loss between the roots), and any tooth lost to periodontitis. A common trap: deep pockets alone never prove periodontitis. Without confirmed bone loss, a mouth full of 4s and 5s could just be widespread gingivitis. Grading answers "how fast is it moving, and how will this patient respond?" Start by assuming Grade B (moderate) and move only if the evidence says so. If old records show change over time, that is the best evidence. If not, take the percent bone loss on the worst tooth and divide by the patient's age: under 0.25 points to Grade A, 0.25 to 1.0 to Grade B, over 1.0 to Grade C. Two things can only push the grade up: heavy smoking (more than 10 cigarettes a day) and an HbA1c of 7% or higher. Either one makes it Grade C even if the ratio says B. Not smoking or not having diabetes never earns a lower grade. Each patient gets one stage (from the single worst site) and one grade. Reading a bone defect When the gum is lifted during surgery, a bone defect is described by how many bony walls are still standing around the damaged root. Picture standing inside the hole and counting the walls around you. A 3-wall defect (cheek side, tongue side, and the wall facing the next tooth are still there; only the root itself is bare) has the best chance of growing bone back. A 2-wall defect has lost one of those walls. When the bone is gone on both sides between the teeth and only the cheek and tongue walls are left, that shape is called a crater. A 1-wall defect has the worst chance. X-rays can fool you here: thick outer bone, especially on the lower jaw, can hide a defect you only see once the gum is lifted. From diagnosis to treatment plan Everyone starts with Phase I (non-surgical care), whatever the stage: hygiene coaching, scaling and root planing (a deep cleaning of the roots), help quitting smoking, fixing fillings or crowns whose edges trap plaque, and cavity treatment. Cavities are easy to forget, but they belong in Phase I, before or alongside the deep cleaning, because a broken-down surface is harder to clean. Permanent crowns or a final partial denture wait until gum treatment is finished; a temporary crown fills the gap. The decision about surgery (Phase II) is made at the Phase I re-evaluation visit, not at the first exam, because that is when you can see how well the gums healed and how well the patient kept up at home. Stage 1-2 cases often clear up with Phase I alone and go straight to maintenance. Stage 3-4 cases more often need surgery: either reshaping bone so it is easy to keep clean (resective surgery) or regrowing bone in a good-shaped defect (regenerative surgery). Every plan ends in maintenance, and the evidence for it is clear: people who refuse treatment lose about three times as many teeth as treated people, and treated people who skip maintenance lose teeth about twice as fast as those who keep their recall visits.
